title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: "She's come to stay with me," said Princess Mary. "The count and countess will be here in a few days. The countess is in a dreadful state, but Natasha herself needed to see a doctor. They insisted she come with me."
"Yes—is there a single family free of sorrow now?" said Pierre, turning to Natasha. "You know it happened on the very day we were rescued. I saw him. What a wonderful boy he was!"
Natasha looked at him, and in answer to his words her eyes widened and lit up.
"What can anyone say, what can anyone think, to console you?" said Pierre. "Nothing! Why did a boy like that, so splendid, so full of life, have to die?"
"Yes, these days it would be hard to live without faith..." Princess Mary remarked.
"Yes, yes, that's really true," Pierre broke in quickly.
"Why is it true?" Natasha asked, looking straight into Pierre's eyes.
"How can you even ask why?" said Princess Mary. "Just the thought of what's waiting for us..."
Natasha, without waiting for Princess Mary to finish, looked questioningly at Pierre again.
"And because," Pierre went on, "only someone who believes there's a God ruling us can bear a loss like hers—and... like yours."
Natasha had already opened her mouth to say something, but stopped herself. Pierre hurriedly turned away from her and went back to questioning Princess Mary about his friend's last days.

Pierre's awkwardness had almost worn off by now, but at the same time he felt that his freedom had vanished completely. He felt that there was now a judge over his every word and action, and that this judge's verdict mattered to him more than the verdict of the whole rest of the world put together. As he spoke, he found himself weighing what impression his words would make on Natasha. He wasn't saying things on purpose to please her, but whatever he said, he looked at it through her eyes.

Princess Mary—reluctantly, as people usually do in such cases—began telling him about the state she'd found Prince Andrew in. But Pierre's face, trembling with feeling, and his eager, restless questions, gradually drew her into details she had dreaded recalling even for her own sake.

"Yes, yes, and then...?" Pierre kept saying, leaning toward her with his whole body, listening eagerly to her story. "Yes, yes... so he grew calm, gentler? With his whole soul he'd always wanted just one thing—to be truly good—so he couldn't have been afraid of dying. Whatever faults he had—if he had any—weren't really his fault. So he did soften?... What a wonderful thing that he saw you again," he added, turning suddenly to Natasha and looking at her with eyes full of tears.
Natasha's face twitched. She frowned and lowered her eyes for a moment. She hesitated, unsure whether to speak.

"Yes, that was happiness," she said at last, in her quiet voice with its deep, chesty tone. "For me, it truly was happiness." She paused. "And he... he... he said he'd been wishing for it at the very moment I walked into the room...."
Natasha's voice broke. She flushed, pressed her clasped hands against her knees, then, with a visible effort at control, lifted her head and began speaking quickly.

"We knew nothing about it when we left Moscow. I didn't dare ask about him. Then suddenly Sonya told me he was traveling with us. I had no idea, I couldn't imagine what state he was in—all I wanted was to see him, to be with him," she said, trembling, breathing fast.

And without letting them interrupt, she went on to tell them what she had never told anyone before—everything she had lived through during those three weeks of the journey and of their time at Yaroslavl.

Pierre listened to her with his lips parted, his tear-filled eyes fixed on her. As he listened he wasn't thinking about Prince Andrew, or about death, or about what she was actually telling him. He listened to her and felt only pity for her—for what she was suffering right now, in the telling.
Princess Mary, frowning as she fought back her own tears, sat beside Natasha and heard, for the first time, the story of those last days of her brother's love for Natasha, and Natasha's for him.
Clearly Natasha needed to tell that story—painful as it was, and joyful too.
She talked on, mixing the most trivial details in with the innermost secrets of her heart, and it seemed as if she would never stop. Several times she repeated the same thing twice.
Dessalles' voice came from outside the door, asking whether little Nicholas could come in to say good night.
"Well, that's all of it—everything," said Natasha.

She got up quickly just as Nicholas came in, almost ran to the door hidden behind the curtains, struck her head on it, and rushed out of the room with a groan of pain or grief—it was hard to tell which.
Pierre stared at the door she had vanished through, and couldn't understand why he suddenly felt utterly alone in the world.
Princess Mary pulled him out of his daze by drawing his attention to her nephew, who had come into the room.

In that moment of tenderness, young Nicholas's face—which looked so much like his father's—moved Pierre so deeply that after kissing the boy he got up quickly, pulled out his handkerchief, and went to the window. He meant to say goodbye to Princess Mary, but she wouldn't let him go.
"No—Natasha and I sometimes don't go to sleep until after two, so please don't leave. I'll have supper brought up. Go on down, we'll join you in a moment."
Before Pierre left the room, Princess Mary told him: "This is the first time she's talked about him like that."
